ground_truth.question_text: Across the first 7.14 million fully driverless miles studied, how often did the automated vehicles experience incidents where someone reportedly sustained an injury, measured per vehicle-miles traveled — and how does that compare with the matched human-driver incidence over the same geography?
ground_truth.answer_text: The any-injury-reported rate was 0.6 incidents per million miles for the ADS vs 2.80 IPMM for the human benchmark when considering all locations together — an 80% reduction, i.e. the human crash rate was 5 times higher than the ADS rate.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Data to Human Benchmarks at 7.1 Million Miles
ground_truth.section_path: A BS T R AC T
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Results: When considering all locations together, the any-injury-reported crashed vehicle rate was 0.6 incidents per million miles (IPMM) for the ADS vs 2.80 IPMM for the human benchmark, an 80% reduction or a human crash rate that is 5 times higher than the ADS rate.

ground_truth.question_text: In the Los Angeles portion of that same rider-only study, how many police-reportable or injury-involved events were actually observed, and what does the study report about the statistical confidence of the comparison there?
ground_truth.answer_text: There were no (zero) police-reported and any-injury-reported crashes in Los Angeles, giving a 0 IPMM point estimate with 95% confidence intervals of (0, 64.1) IPMM; the single SGO crash there met the any-property-damage-or-injury threshold but the low mileage meant comparisons were not statistically significant.

ground_truth.question_text: How did the authors assemble a single human comparison group spanning Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles, given that their benchmark rates came from separate city-level analyses?
ground_truth.answer_text: They combined the human crash benchmarks for Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles proportional to the miles driven in the Waymo RO service (a mileage blended average); for confidence-interval purposes the blended benchmark used 19,002 million VMT.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Data to Human Benchmarks at 7.1 Million Miles
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The human crash benchmarks reported in Scanlon et al. (2023) for Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles were combined proportional to the miles driven in the Waymo RO service, as shown in Table 3.

ground_truth.question_text: Which statistical method did the study use for confidence intervals on the ratio of automated-vehicle to human event rates, and why was it preferred over a resampling-based alternative?
ground_truth.answer_text: Rate-ratio confidence intervals used the Nelson (1970) method based on a Poisson model. A parametric bootstrap using CRSS survey-design standard errors produced narrower intervals, so the Nelson method was kept because it is more conservative (wider CIs).
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Data to Human Benchmarks at 7.1 Million Miles
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The Nelson (1970) method is more conservative (i.e., produces larger confidence intervals) relative to the parametric boostrap method.
ground_truth.provenance: Excerpt located and extracted programmatically from waymo/data/papers.db chunks.text via the builder's normalized-substring resolver (2026-08-22); gold_block_id taken from the resolved chunk's own anchor_json. Note 'boostrap' typo is verbatim in the stored chunk.

ground_truth.question_text: Two corpus papers benchmark the same driverless service at different exposure levels. How did the headline police-reported reduction estimate change between the roughly 7-million-mile analysis and the later 56.7-million-mile analysis, and what happened to the uncertainty around it?
ground_truth.answer_text: The earlier 7.1M-mile study found a 55% reduction in police-reported crashes (95% CI 22% to 77%); the 56.7M-mile follow-up found a 65% reduction (95% CI 57% to 72%) — a similar point estimate with much tighter confidence intervals.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Kusano et al (2024) found a statistically significant reduction in Police-Reported (55% reduction, 22% to 77% 95% confidence interval) and Any-Injury-Reported (80% reduction, 44% to 96% 95% confidence interval) in all locations combined.

ground_truth.question_text: Did every front-to-rear collision outcome move in the safer direction for the automated fleet at 56.7 million miles? Identify any sub-category where the automated vehicles did significantly worse than the human comparison, with numbers.
ground_truth.answer_text: Yes, one went the other way: there was a statistically significant increase in F2R Struck Any-Injury-Reported crashes in Phoenix (+117%, 95% CI 11% to 281%). Overall F2R striking fell significantly while struck crashes rose or held steady, leaving overall F2R rates similar in magnitude to the benchmark.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles

ground_truth.question_text: Before impact, how was the automated vehicle typically moving in rear-end events where it was hit from behind? Give the movement categories the authors defined, their kinematic thresholds, and how the events distributed across them.
ground_truth.answer_text: Pre-crash movement was classified into three categories: (a) stopped for more than 5 seconds prior to the crash, (b) traveling at constant speed or accelerating (decelerations less than 0.75 m/s^2 in the prior 5 seconds), or (c) braking with peak magnitude less than 3.5 m/s^2 over the prior 5 seconds. In 100% of Airbag Deployment and 76% of Any-Injury-Reported F2R Struck crashes the vehicle was stopped, at constant speed, or decelerating with traffic; the remaining 24% had braking above 3.5 m/s^2.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The pre-crash movement was classified into three categories: (a) the ADS vehicle was stopped for more than 5 second prior to the crash, (b) the ADS vehicle was traveling at a constant speed (decelerations less than 0.75 m/s<sup>2</sup> in the 5 seconds prior to the crash) or accelerating and (c) braking with peak magnitude less than 3.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> for the 5 seconds prior to a crash.

ground_truth.question_text: An insurance-industry analysis in this corpus measured driverless-vehicle safety using third-party liability claims rather than police reports. What reductions did it report against its newest-vehicle human comparison group, and why does the 56.7-million-mile crash-rate study say those claim-based figures cannot be compared head-to-head with its own?
ground_truth.answer_text: Di Lillo et al. (2024b) found an 86% reduction in property damage claims and a 90% reduction in bodily injury claims versus latest-generation (model years 2018-2021) human-driven vehicles over 25.3 million rider-only miles. The 56.7M-mile study notes these are slightly higher than its own crash-rate reductions but not directly comparable, because liability claims are a subset of all crashes where the insured party has some contribution to the cause.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Di Lillo et al (2024b) compared the Waymo RO 3rd party liability property damage and bodily injury claims rates to a benchmark of human insured latest-generation vehicles (model years 2018-2021).

supporting_sources.passage_excerpt: Results demonstrate that the Waymo ADS significantly outperformed both the overall driving population (88% reduction in property damage claims, 92% in bodily injury claims), and outperformed the more stringent latest-generation HDV benchmark (86% reduction in property damage claims and 90% in bodily injury claims).

ground_truth.question_text: Which severity outcome in the 56.7-million-mile analysis flips its statistical conclusion depending on whether the human comparison rates are re-weighted to match where and when the automated fleet actually drove? Describe both conclusions.
ground_truth.answer_text: Suspected Serious Injury+. Without the dynamic benchmark adjustment the reduction was NOT statistically significant in Phoenix or San Francisco (only in all locations combined); with the dynamic adjustment it was significant in Phoenix, San Francisco, and all locations combined. The authors therefore present Suspected Serious Injury+ as indicative, unlike the more certain Any-Injury-Reported and Airbag Deployment outcomes.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles
ground_truth.section_path: Underreporting and Dynamic Benchmark Sensitivity Study
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Without the dynamic benchmark adjustment, the reductions in Suspected Serious Injury+ crashes was not statistically significant in Phoenix or San Francisco but was statistically significant in all locations combined, whereas it was statistically significant in Phoenix, San Francisco, and in all locations combined with the dynamic adjustment.

ground_truth.question_text: For controlled-access highways, how much did the rate of injury-involving collisions vary across the US metro areas benchmarked, quoting the extreme cities and the spread?
ground_truth.answer_text: Freeway any-injury-reported crash rates showed large geographic variation: nearly 3.5 times higher in Atlanta (2.4 IPMM, the highest) compared to Phoenix (0.7 IPMM, the lowest).

ground_truth.question_text: What statistical power setup did the freeway-benchmark study use when computing how many miles an automated fleet must drive before its difference from human drivers becomes detectable, and which effect sizes were considered?
ground_truth.answer_text: A power analysis modeling asymptotic normal approximations to a Poisson distribution, targeting 80% statistical power with two-sided tests at alpha = 0.05. Evaluated ADS performance levels were 25%, 50%, 75%, and 90% reductions in crash rates and 25% and 50% increases. Required mileage is inversely proportional to the benchmark crash rate.

ground_truth.question_text: In Waymo's earliest published safety-performance report, how many physical contacts — real or reconstructed in counterfactual replay — occurred across the covered operations, and how do the real and simulated counts break down?
ground_truth.answer_text: 47 contact events in total: 18 actual and 29 simulated contact events, none expected to result in severe or life-threatening injuries.

ground_truth.question_text: According to that early report, which collision modes did the automated driver completely avoid — modes that human-driven vehicles are frequently involved in — and in how many events was the automated vehicle itself the party that hit a pedestrian or cyclist?
ground_truth.answer_text: It completely avoided road departure, contact with fixed objects/roadway infrastructure, and rollover (zero actual or simulated such events), and there were no collisions in which the Waymo Driver struck a pedestrian or cyclist. There were three events (one actual, two simulated) in which the Waymo vehicle was struck by a pedestrian or cyclist while stopped.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Waymo Public Road Safety Performance Data

ground_truth.question_text: Of the most serious tier of events in the 2019-era public-road safety data — those involving airbag deployment in any vehicle — how many were genuine versus simulated, and did any reach the two highest ISO 26262 severity classes?
ground_truth.answer_text: Eight airbag-deployment-level S1 events: five were simulated with expected deployment, two actual events involved deployment of only another vehicle's frontal airbags, and one actual event involved another vehicle's frontal airbags plus the Waymo vehicle's side airbags. There were no actual or predicted S2 or S3 events.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Waymo Public Road Safety Performance Data

ground_truth.question_text: Waymo's cumulative public-road mileage appears in several corpus papers at different dates. Reconstruct that timeline: the figure reported in the original open-dataset-era safety paper, the rider-only figure through January 2025, and the milestone reported as reached in July 2025.
ground_truth.answer_text: Over 20 million miles on public roads since testing began in 2009 (Waymo Public Road Safety Performance Data); over 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025 (brake-onset paper citing Kusano et al. 2025), quickly reaching 100 million miles in July 2025 (per Waymo), surpassing SHRP2's mileage.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Automated Brake Onset Detection in Naturalistic Driving Data
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: For example, Waymo has accumulated over 56.7 million miles of rider-only self-driving miles through January 2025 (Kusano et al., 2025) and quickly reached 100 million miles in July 2025 (Waymo, 2025) , surpassing the mileage covered in the second Strategic Highway Research Program (SHRP2) (Dingus et al., 2015; Perez et al., 2016).
